title: Animation Performance & Best Practices ⚡
description: Write high‑performance animations, respect user preferences, and debug with DevTools.

slides.title: The 60fps Goal 🎯
slides.content:
# Smooth Animations Need Efficient Code

Browsers aim to render at 60 frames per second (fps). To achieve smooth animations, you must avoid triggering expensive layout recalculations (reflow) or repaints.

The cheapest properties to animate are `transform` and `opacity`. They only trigger compositing, which runs on the GPU. Avoid animating `width`, `left`, `margin`, `padding`, which cause layout thrashing.

slides.title: Using `will-change` 🚀

quizData.question: Animating `width` instead of `transform: scaleX()` is more performant.
quizData.explanation: `width` triggers layout recalculations; `transform` is compositor‑only and far more performant.

slides.title: The `prefers-reduced-motion` Media Query ♿
Debugging with DevTools 🛠️
slides.content:
# Visualise Animation Performance

Chrome DevTools:
- **Animations tab** (Customize and control → More tools → Animations) lets you inspect, slow down, and scrub through animations.
- **Performance panel** records frames to see which properties cause layout or paint.
- **Rendering tab** (More tools → Rendering) can highlight paint rectangles and FPS meter.

Firefox: Animation inspector and frame‑by‑frame scrubbing.

slides.title: Reduced Motion Example
Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use the Compositor

Keep animations on the GPU: only change `transform` and `opacity`. Use `requestAnimationFrame()` in JS for more complex logic, but CSS animations are often enough.
